controlOptions.title: Let the preamplifier switch it
controlOptions.summary: The way Gryphon intend it to work: an upstream preamplifier with a 12 V trigger output drives the amplifier's 12 V Link input, so the amplifier follows the preamplifier in and out of standby with no extra hardware. If the preamplifier is itself controllable — over RS-232, for instance — then controlling it controls the amplifier.

requires.name: An upstream device with a 12 V trigger output that can itself be switched
requires.note: Usually the preamplifier. It has to be genuinely controllable, otherwise this only moves the manual switch one box upstream.

requires.name: Mono mini-jack cable from the preamplifier's trigger output to the amplifier's 12 V Link input

controlOptions.limitations: Power and standby only. Mute and the three Class A bias settings stay on the front panel whatever you do, and there is no way to read the amplifier's state back — the trigger is a signal you assert, not a conversation.
controlOptions.caution: Bring the power amplifier up LAST and take it down FIRST. A power amplifier switched on while its source is still settling can pass a turn-on thump to the speakers.

controlOptions.title: Network relay switching a 12 V supply
controlOptions.summary: Where nothing upstream offers a trigger output, a network-controlled relay can make one. The relay does not generate the voltage itself — it switches an external 12 V DC supply into the amplifier's 12 V Link input, and holding the relay closed holds the amplifier on.

requires.name: A relay module controllable over the network

examples.name: Global Caché iTach IP2CC

examples.name: Shelly Plus 1
examples.note: Inexpensive WiFi relay with a potential-free contact mode.

requires.note: What matters is that it gives a genuinely dry, potential-free contact — not a switched mains output.

requires.name: A 12 V DC power supply
requires.note: This is the part people leave out. A relay closes a circuit but sources no voltage, so a relay wired straight across the trigger jack does nothing at all and the amplifier looks broken.

controlOptions.wiring: Take the 12 V supply's positive through the relay's normally-open contact and on to the tip of a mono mini-jack; take the supply's negative to the sleeve. Closing the relay applies 12 V and the amplifier leaves standby; opening it returns the amplifier to standby. Keep the supply's ground common with the jack sleeve and nothing else.
controlOptions.limitations: Power and standby only, and still no state readback: Lyr knows whether it closed the relay, which is not the same as knowing the amplifier came up.
controlOptions.caution: Check the amplifier's tolerance before applying anything other than 12 V — Gryphon publish no accepted range for this input, so treat 12 V as the only safe figure. Confirm the relay is a dry contact and not switched mains before it goes anywhere near a signal jack.

controlOptions.title: Mute and bias stay manual
controlOptions.summary: Nothing reaches the rest of the amplifier. Mute and the three Class A bias settings are on the front panel only — there is no serial port, no infrared receiver and no network interface to carry them, so no adapter or bridge can expose them.

ir.note: Schiit ship ONE remote for the whole preamp line: "It's the same one we use for all Sagas, Freyas, and Kara" (Saga 2 manual, Remote Control). So a frame meant for one of them reaches every other one in the room, and each unit needs its own emitter over its IR window rather than a shared blaster. Schiit do not publish the codes themselves — the manuals document the five buttons (Input, Volume Up, Volume Down, Output, Mute) and nothing about protocol or values — so commands here have to be captured from the physical remote. Protocol and address are a hardware capture, not a Schiit document: read off the supplied remote on 2026-09-08 with a USB IR Toy v2 on /dev/lirc0 (scripts/link/ir-capture.py, raw log in data/ir-captures/). Extended NEC, 16-bit address 0x1BF1, five distinct commands 0xF1-0xF5 — one per button, which matches the five buttons the manuals describe. Because every Saga, Freya and Kara answers this one remote, a frame reaches all of them: fit an emitter over each unit's window rather than using a shared blaster. 38 kHz is the NEC nominal carrier, not a measured value.

ir.note: Schiit ship ONE remote for the whole preamp line: "It's the same one we use for all Sagas, Freyas, and Kara" (Saga 2 manual, Remote Control). So a frame meant for one of them reaches every other one in the room, and each unit needs its own emitter over its IR window rather than a shared blaster. Schiit do not publish the codes themselves — the manuals document the five buttons (Input, Volume Up, Volume Down, Output, Mute) and nothing about protocol or values — so commands here have to be captured from the physical remote. Protocol and address are a hardware capture, not a Schiit document: read off the supplied remote on 2026-09-08 with a USB IR Toy v2 on /dev/lirc0 (scripts/link/ir-capture.py, raw log in data/ir-captures/). Extended NEC, 16-bit address 0x1BF1, five distinct commands 0xF1-0xF5 — one per button, which matches the five buttons the manuals describe. Because every Saga, Freya and Kara answers this one remote, a frame reaches all of them: fit an emitter over each unit's window rather than using a shared blaster. 38 kHz is the NEC nominal carrier, not a measured value.

metadata.notes: Passive or JFET-buffered output — so its Output button cycles two modes, not three. Icon: the generic amplifier chassis, not a Schiit fascia. This library's glyphs are pixel-measured off a straight-on front elevation, and Schiit publish only three-quarter renders (freyaplus-LISST-front-1920.jpg, kara-front-blk-1920.jpg are both in perspective), so a measured Freya/Saga/Kara fascia is still owed a square-on photograph.
